entry.title: Compound Risk is a Bigger Problem Than Missing Checks
entry.summary:
Two different problems
Security tools have blind spots. AWS Trusted Advisor can't detect incomplete observation data, latent exposure behind Public Access Block, or ACL escalation paths. Those are real gaps. If your tool doesn't check for something, you won't find it. But there's a bigger problem that gets less attention: the tool checks for things individually and misses what happens when they combine. This is compound risk. It's not a missing check — it's a missing dimension of analysis. Trusted Advisor evaluates settings one at a time: Is this bucket public? Yes/No. Is encryption enabled? Yes/No. Is logging turned on? Yes/No. Each check returns an independent result. The results don't talk to each other. entry.title: Eval-Driven Development for AI Agent Skills
entry.summary:
The Problem with Writing Skills by Hand
You've written a skill for your AI coding agent. It's got clear instructions, proper formatting, a good description. You test it in a session — it works. Ship it, right? Not so fast. Skills trigger based on their description field — a 1-2 sentence summary in the SKILL.md frontmatter. And here's the thing: descriptions that seem crystal clear to humans often trigger wrong. Too specific, and the skill never activates when it should. Too broad, and it fires on unrelated prompts. The result: skills that feel right in theory but fail unpredictably in practice. And there's no systematic way to measure whether a skill is getting better or worse across iterations. This is the same problem software engineering solved decades ago with automated testing. Skil…

entry.title: Building a Voice-Controlled Local AI Agent
entry.summary:
I built a voice-controlled AI agent that takes audio input, understands user intent, executes local tools safely, and shows every step in a simple web UI. The system follows a pipeline design: Input Layer
The user can either record audio from a microphone or upload an audio file (.wav/.mp3).
I also added a text-input tab for quick debugging and testing.
Speech-to-Text (STT)
Audio is sent to AssemblyAI for transcription.
Intent Understanding
The transcription is passed to a Groq-hosted LLM, which classifies it into structured intents: create_file write_code summarize general_chat The classifier returns JSON so tool routing is deterministic. Tool Execution Layer
Based on intents, the app triggers tools: file/folder creation code generation + save summarization chat response Safety + UI Layer
All writes are restricted to an output/ folder.
A human-in-the-loop confirmation checkbox is required before file operations execute.
The UI displays: transcribed text detected intent(s) action taken final result I used AssemblyAI for speech recognition instead of running Whisper locally.
Why: fast setup and high accuracy works well without local GPU generous free tier (330 hours), which is practical for development/testing I used Groq for intent classification and generation tasks.
Why: very fast inference latency reliable structured output for JSON intent classification same model family can handle classification, summarization, code generation, and chat A key issue was transcription config compatibility: speech_model became deprecated API expected speech_models (list form) valid values were strict ("universal-3-pro", "universal-2") I fixed this by using:
python speech_models=["universal-3-pro", "universal-2"]
